items.stem: A server has 4,000 MB of RAM. The operating system, nginx and the database already use 1,000 MB. You want to keep 15% of the RAM free, and each worker needs 200 MB. About how many workers can you run?

options.feedback: Keeping 15% free leaves 3,400 MB. Taking away the 1,000 MB already in use leaves 2,400 MB, and 2,400 divided by 200 is 12.
This divides 3,000 MB by 200 and forgets the 15% that should stay free. Without free memory the system has no disk cache and slows down.
This divides 3,400 MB by 200 and forgets that the operating system, nginx and the database already use 1,000 MB.
This divides all 4,000 MB by 200. Part of the RAM is already in use before the first worker starts.

items.stem: Before you try it: the machine has 2 GB of RAM, the database is on the same machine, and each worker uses 90 MB plus 8 MB for the request it is handling. You raise the number of workers from 8 to 20. What will the memory bar show?

options.text: The bar shows more used memory but plenty still free.
options.feedback: Twenty workers need about 1,960 MB on top of roughly 780 MB that the operating system, nginx and database use. That is more than the 2,048 MB available.

options.text: The bar shows the machine is over capacity.
options.feedback: Twenty workers need about 1,960 MB and the other programs use about 780 MB. The total is more than 2,048 MB, so the operating system would stop a process.

options.text: The bar stays the same, because the workers share memory.
options.feedback: Each worker is a separate process with its own copy of the application, so memory use grows with every worker. Only the preload switch lets them share some of it.

items.try: Drag the Workers slider to 20 and read the message under the memory bar.

items.stem: An application spends most of each request waiting for the database. You want it to handle more requests at once without a large increase in memory. What is a reasonable step?

options.text: Run several threads inside each worker.
options.feedback: Threads in one process share its memory, so they cost little extra. Waiting for the database does not need two threads to run Python code at the same moment.
This would work, but each new worker is a separate process with its own copy of the application. The memory cost is large.

options.text: Turn off the disk cache to free memory.
options.feedback: The disk cache is memory the system uses to avoid reading files from the slow disk. Removing it makes the machine slower and does not add capacity.

options.text: Nothing helps, because Python cannot handle two requests at once.
options.feedback: Processes can run in parallel, and threads can overlap their waiting. The limit applies only to running Python code in two threads at the same moment.

items.stem: The application machine already has plenty of free RAM and its workers are not short of memory. Which reason still supports moving Postgres to its own machine?

options.text: The database can be backed up and restarted without affecting the application.
options.feedback: Separate machines can be maintained separately, and a runaway query cannot use up the application's memory. These are operational reasons that do not depend on spare RAM.

options.text: Queries become faster because the network is quicker than the same machine.
options.feedback: A query that crosses a network takes longer, about 0.4 ms more in this model. It never gets faster than a query inside the machine.

options.text: The monthly cost goes down, because each machine is smaller.
options.feedback: Two machines cost about twice as much as one in this model.

options.text: More workers will fit on the application machine.
options.feedback: This only helps when memory was the limit. Here the application machine already has free RAM.

items.stem: Before you try it: you set Total RAM to 16 GB, so the application machine has plenty of memory. Will moving Postgres to its own machine lower the cost per request per second?

options.text: Yes, because the database gets a whole machine.
options.feedback: A faster database helps a little, but the cost doubles. With this much memory the workers were not short of it, so throughput grows only slightly.

options.text: No, the cost per request per second goes up.
options.feedback: The second machine doubles the monthly cost, and throughput rises by only about 15% in the model. The cost for each request per second therefore goes up.

options.text: It stays the same, because the total RAM is the same.
options.feedback: The total RAM doubles, because the database gets its own 16 GB machine, and the monthly cost doubles with it.

items.try: Drag the Total RAM slider to 16 GB and read the bottom row of the comparison table.
